summary.text: At \(n=67\), both \(m=147\) and \(m=2^{67}+1\) give the defining sum \(67\): the residues of 147 modulo \(2,4,\ldots,128\) are \(1,3,3,3,19,19,19\), while the 67 relevant residues of \(2^{67}+1\) are all \(1\). Thus there are at least two occurrences, contradicting the asserted uniqueness.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor\log_2 m\rfloor}(m\bmod 2^k).
\]
Thus, for positive \(n\), the quantity \(a(n)\) in the conjecture is the number of integers \(m\) in the finite search range
\[
0\le m<2^{n+1}
\]
for which \(F(m)=n\). (The separate \(n=0\) branch in the definition is irrelevant here.)

We disprove the assertion at the listed value \(n=67\). We will exhibit two distinct integers in the defining search range for \(a(67)\), both having \(F(m)=67\).

First take
\[
m_1=147.
\]
Since
\[
2^7=128\le147<256=2^8,
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 147\rfloor=7\). The seven residues occurring in \(F(147)\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccc}
k&1&2&3&4&5&6&7\\ \hline
147\bmod 2^k&1&3&3&3&19&19&19.
\end{array}
\]
Indeed, \(147\equiv1\pmod2\); \(147=144+3\), with \(144\) divisible by \(4,8,16\); and \(147=128+19\), giving remainder \(19\) modulo \(32,64,128\). Consequently
\[
F(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67.
\]
Also \(147<2^{68}\), so \(147\) lies in the search range used to define \(a(67)\).

For the second integer, take the standard “trivial” input
\[
m_2=2^{67}+1.
\]
Because
\[
2^{67}\le 2^{67}+1<2^{68},
\]
we have
\[
\lfloor\log_2(2^{67}+1)\rfloor=67.
\]
For every \(k\) with \(1\le k\le67\), the number \(2^k\) divides \(2^{67}\). Hence
\[
2^{67}+1\equiv1\pmod{2^k}.
\]
Since \(1<2^k\), the actual remainder is exactly \(1\). All 67 terms in the defining sum are therefore equal to \(1\), and so
\[
F(2^{67}+1)=\sum_{k=1}^{67}1=67.
\]
The inequality above also shows directly that \(m_2<2^{68}\), so this second integer is likewise in the search range for \(a(67)\).

The two inputs are distinct: \(147<2^{67}+1\). Thus the set
\[
\{m:0\le m<2^{68},\ F(m)=67\}
\]
contains at least the two distinct elements \(147\) and \(2^{67}+1\). Its cardinality is therefore at least \(2\). By the definition of the sequence term,
\[
a(67)\ge2,
\]
and in particular
\[
a(67)\ne1.
\]

Finally, \(67\) is one of the elements of the conjecture’s set
\[
\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}.
\]
The conjecture says that every element \(n\) of this set satisfies \(a(n)=1\), so it would imply \(a(67)=1\). This contradicts the two explicit occurrences above. Therefore the conjecture is false.
